sections.title: Free oscillation: $my'' + ky = 0$
sections.summary: A mass on a spring with no friction oscillates forever at the natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m}$. Two initial conditions fix the two constants: $y = y(0)\cos\omega_n t + \dfrac{y'(0)}{\omega_n}\sin\omega_n t$.
goals: Explain why a second order equation needs two initial conditions.
Find the null solutions $\cos\omega_n t$ and $\sin\omega_n t$ of $my'' + ky = 0$.
Match $c_1$ and $c_2$ to $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$, and write the answer as $R\cos(\omega_n t - \alpha)$.
Relate $\omega$ (radians per second), frequency $f = \omega/2\pi$ (hertz) and period $T = 2\pi/\omega$.

notes.heading: Two derivatives, two conditions
paragraphs: Newton's law $F = ma$ makes acceleration $y''$ the natural unknown in mechanics. A second order equation $Ay'' + By' + Cy = f(t)$ has two null solutions, so its complete solution $y = y_p + c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$ has two constants. They come from two initial conditions: the starting position $y(0)$ and the starting velocity $y'(0)$.
In this unit the coefficients are constants: $A = m$ (mass), $B = b$ (damping) and $C = k$ (spring constant).

notes.heading: No damping, no force
paragraphs: With $B = 0$ and $f = 0$, $my'' + ky = 0$ says the spring force $-ky$ is the only force. Divide by $m$: $y'' + \omega_n^2 y = 0$ with $\omega_n^2 = k/m$. We need functions whose second derivative is $-\omega_n^2$ times themselves: $\cos\omega_n t$ and $\sin\omega_n t$.
Then $y = c_1\cos\omega_n t + c_2\sin\omega_n t$. At $t = 0$ the cosine is $1$ and the sine is $0$, so $c_1 = y(0)$. The derivative at $0$ is $c_2\omega_n$, so $c_2 = y'(0)/\omega_n$.

notes.heading: One cosine with a phase
paragraphs: A sum of a cosine and a sine with the same frequency is one shifted cosine: $c_1\cos\omega t + c_2\sin\omega t = R\cos(\omega t - \alpha)$ with $R = \sqrt{c_1^2 + c_2^2}$ and $\tan\alpha = c_2/c_1$. The amplitude $R$ never changes: energy (kinetic plus potential) is conserved when there is no friction.
Units matter. $\omega$ is in radians per second; the frequency $f = \omega/2\pi$ counts full cycles per second (hertz); the period is $T = 2\pi/\omega = 1/f$.

notes.heading: The exponential form
paragraphs: Euler's formula gives the same null solutions as $e^{i\omega_n t}$ and $e^{-i\omega_n t}$. Substituting $y = e^{st}$ gives $ms^2 + k = 0$, so $s = \pm i\omega_n$: pure imaginary exponents mean pure oscillation. Section 3 adds damping and the exponents get a negative real part.

sections.title: Forcing $\cos\omega t$ and the impulse response
sections.summary: Driving $my'' + ky = \cos\omega t$ gives the particular solution $Y\cos\omega t$ with $Y = \dfrac{1}{m(\omega_n^2 - \omega^2)}$, which explodes as $\omega \to \omega_n$ (resonance). A hammer blow $\delta(t)$ gives the impulse response $g(t) = \dfrac{\sin\omega_n t}{m\,\omega_n}$.
goals: Find the particular solution of $my'' + ky = \cos\omega t$ by trying $Y\cos\omega t$.
Explain the frequency response $1/(m(\omega_n^2 - \omega^2))$ and resonance $\omega = \omega_n$.
Turn $my'' + ky = \delta(t)$ into a null problem with $g(0) = 0$, $g'(0) = 1/m$, and solve it.

notes.heading: Try a cosine
paragraphs: The input $\cos\omega t$ has a frequency $\omega$ set from outside; the spring has its own natural frequency $\omega_n$. Try $y_p = Y\cos\omega t$. Two derivatives give $-\omega^2 Y\cos\omega t$, and there is no $y'$ term to bring in a sine, so cosines alone balance: $-m\omega^2 Y + kY = 1$.
Hence $Y = \dfrac{1}{k - m\omega^2} = \dfrac{1}{m(\omega_n^2 - \omega^2)}$ using $k = m\omega_n^2$. This number, as a function of $\omega$, is the frequency response.

notes.heading: Complete solution and resonance
paragraphs: $y = Y\cos\omega t + c_1\cos\omega_n t + c_2\sin\omega_n t$: two frequencies together. The constants come from $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$, not from $Y$. Starting from rest, $y = Y(\cos\omega t - \cos\omega_n t)$.

When $\omega$ is close to $\omega_n$ the denominator $\omega_n^2 - \omega^2$ is small and $Y$ is large: the system is pushed at almost its own rhythm. At $\omega = \omega_n$ the formula breaks down; that case, resonance, needs an extra factor $t$ (Section 5).

notes.heading: A sudden blow
paragraphs: $my'' + ky = \delta(t)$ means an impulse at $t = 0$, starting from rest. For $t > 0$ there is no force, so $g$ is a null solution. The delta function changes the momentum $mg'$ by $1$ at the instant $t = 0$: the problem is the same as $mg'' + kg = 0$ with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1/m$.
Using Section 1 with $c_1 = 0$, $c_2 = (1/m)/\omega_n$: $g(t) = \dfrac{\sin\omega_n t}{m\,\omega_n}$. This impulse response returns in Section 4 and in the Laplace transform unit.

sections.title: Damping: the roots of $As^2 + Bs + C = 0$
sections.summary: With damping, $y = e^{st}$ gives $As^2 + Bs + C = 0$. The sign of $B^2 - 4AC$ sorts the motion: overdamped (two negative real roots), critically damped (a double root, solutions $e^{st}$ and $te^{st}$), underdamped (complex roots $-B/2A \pm i\omega_d$, a decaying oscillation).
goals: Substitute $y = e^{st}$ and get the characteristic equation $As^2 + Bs + C = 0$.
Classify the four cases by $B$ and $B^2 - 4AC$.
Write the null solutions in each case, including $te^{st}$ for a double root.
Read the roots from the graph of the parabola $As^2 + Bs + C$.

notes.heading: The characteristic equation
paragraphs: Unforced means $f = 0$. Put $y = e^{st}$ into $Ay'' + By' + Cy = 0$: every term carries $e^{st}$, which is never zero, so $As^2 + Bs + C = 0$. The quadratic formula gives $s_{1,2} = \dfrac{-B \pm \sqrt{B^2 - 4AC}}{2A}$, and $y = c_1e^{s_1t} + c_2e^{s_2t}$.
Two useful checks: $s_1 + s_2 = -B/A$ and $s_1s_2 = C/A = \omega_n^2$.

notes.heading: Four cases
paragraphs: Undamped, $B = 0$: $s = \pm i\omega_n$, pure oscillation (Section 1).

Underdamped, $B^2 < 4AC$: $s = -\dfrac{B}{2A} \pm i\omega_d$ with $\omega_d = \sqrt{\dfrac{C}{A} - \dfrac{B^2}{4A^2}}$. The solution $e^{-Bt/2A}(c_1\cos\omega_d t + c_2\sin\omega_d t)$ oscillates while it decays; damping also slows the oscillation, $\omega_d < \omega_n$.
Critically damped, $B^2 = 4AC$: one double root $s = -B/2A$. The second solution is $te^{st}$.
Overdamped, $B^2 > 4AC$: two different negative real roots, two decaying exponentials and no oscillation.

notes.heading: Roots from a parabola
paragraphs: Strang graphs $As^2 + Bs + C$ against $s$. For $s^2 + 2s$ it crosses zero at $0$ and $-2$. Raise it by $1$: $s^2 + 2s + 1 = (s+1)^2$ just touches zero at $-1$, a double root. Raise it again: $s^2 + 2s + 2$ never reaches zero, and the roots $-1 \pm i$ are complex. Increasing $C$ (a stiffer spring) moves the motion from overdamped through critical to underdamped.

notes.heading: Damping ratio
paragraphs: The case is decided by one dimensionless number, the damping ratio $\zeta = \dfrac{B}{\sqrt{4AC}}$: $\zeta = 0$ undamped, $\zeta < 1$ underdamped, $\zeta = 1$ critical, $\zeta > 1$ overdamped (Section 6).

example.title: An underdamped spring (authored)
example.answer: $y = e^{-t}(\cos 2t + \tfrac12\sin 2t)$, oscillating at $\omega_d = 2$ inside the envelope $\pm\tfrac{\sqrt5}{2}e^{-t}$ (here $\omega_n = \sqrt5$). The decay factor is $e^{-t}$; the amplitude $\sqrt{1 + 1/4} = \sqrt5/2$ comes from the two coefficients.

sections.title: Impulse response $g(t)$ and step response $r(t)$
sections.summary: For $y'' + By' + Cy$, the impulse response is $g = \dfrac{e^{s_1t} - e^{s_2t}}{s_1 - s_2}$ (from $g(0) = 0$, $g'(0) = 1$). The step response, the answer to a unit step from rest, is the integral of $g$: $r(t) = \dfrac{1}{C} + \dfrac{s_2e^{s_1t} - s_1e^{s_2t}}{C(s_1 - s_2)}$.
goals: Solve $g'' + Bg' + Cg = \delta(t)$ by the equivalent conditions $g(0) = 0$, $g'(0) = 1$.
Specialise $g$ to the undamped, underdamped and critical cases.
Find the step response $r(t)$ and check that $r' = g$.

notes.heading: The impulse response
paragraphs: With $A = 1$, the impulse $\delta(t)$ starts the system from rest with velocity $1$. So $g$ is the null solution with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$. In $g = c_1e^{s_1t} + c_2e^{s_2t}$: $c_1 + c_2 = 0$ and $c_1s_1 + c_2s_2 = 1$, so $c_1 = -c_2 = 1/(s_1 - s_2)$:
$g(t) = \dfrac{e^{s_1t} - e^{s_2t}}{s_1 - s_2}.$ This is a difference quotient, and that explains the special cases.

notes.heading: The special cases
paragraphs: No damping: $s = \pm i\omega_n$ and $g = \dfrac{\sin\omega_n t}{\omega_n}$ (Section 2 with $m = 1$). Underdamped: $s = -\tfrac{B}{2} \pm i\omega_d$ and $g = e^{-Bt/2}\dfrac{\sin\omega_d t}{\omega_d}$. Critical damping: $s_2 \to s_1$, and the difference quotient becomes a derivative with respect to $s$: $g = te^{s_1t} = te^{-Bt/2}$.

notes.heading: The step response
paragraphs: Now the input is a unit step $H(t)$, switched on at $t = 0$ from rest: $r'' + Br' + Cr = 1$ with $r(0) = r'(0) = 0$. A constant particular solution is $1/C$. The null part must cancel the starting value $1/C$ and keep the slope $0$. That gives
$r(t) = \dfrac{1}{C} + \dfrac{s_2e^{s_1t} - s_1e^{s_2t}}{C\,(s_1 - s_2)}$, using $s_1s_2 = C$. In the lecture the board is written for $C = 1$, where the leading term is $1$.
The step is the integral of the delta function, so the step response is the integral of the impulse response: $r(t) = \int_0^t g(s)\,ds$. With damping, $r(t)$ settles at $1/C$.

example.title: Overdamped responses (authored)

steps.text: Step response: integrate g from 0 to t (or use the formula with C = 2).

example.answer: $g = e^{-t} - e^{-2t}$ and $r = \tfrac12 - e^{-t} + \tfrac12e^{-2t}$; indeed $r' = g$ and $r \to 1/C = \tfrac12$.

sections.title: Exponential input: $Y = 1/P(s)$ and resonance
sections.summary: For $P(D)y = e^{st}$, the particular solution is $y_p = e^{st}/P(s)$, where $P(s) = As^2 + Bs + C$ and $1/P(s)$ is the transfer function. If $s$ is a root of $P$ (resonance) the formula fails and $y_p = \dfrac{te^{st}}{P'(s)}$.
goals: Find $Y = 1/P(s)$ by substituting $Ye^{st}$, for any order.
Recognise resonance: the input exponent equals a null exponent.
Derive $te^{st}/P'(s)$ by letting $s$ approach the root (l'Hôpital).

notes.heading: The transfer function
paragraphs: Write $D = d/dt$ and $P(D) = AD^2 + BD + C$; the same idea works for any degree $N$. Since $D e^{st} = se^{st}$, the input $e^{st}$ passes through $P(D)$ as multiplication by $P(s)$: $P(D)(Ye^{st}) = YP(s)e^{st}$. Matching $e^{st}$ gives $Y = 1/P(s)$, the transfer function. One division solves the problem.

notes.heading: Resonance
paragraphs: The formula fails when $P(s) = 0$, that is, when $s$ is one of the null exponents $s_1, s_2$. Then $e^{st}$ already solves the null equation and cannot produce a nonzero right side. This is resonance: the input exponent hits a pole of $1/P$.

notes.heading: Finding the new solution
paragraphs: Take $s$ close to $s_1$ and use the particular solution that starts like a null solution: $y = \dfrac{e^{st} - e^{s_1t}}{P(s)}$. It still solves $P(D)y = e^{st}$, because the subtracted term is a null solution. As $s \to s_1$ it is $0/0$. L'Hôpital's rule, differentiating top and bottom with respect to $s$, gives
$y_p = \dfrac{te^{s_1t}}{P'(s_1)}$, and for a second order equation $P'(s) = 2As + B$. The extra factor $t$ is the signature of resonance. A double root ($P'(s_1) = 0$ too) brings $t^2$.

sections.title: Cosine forcing with damping: gain $G$ and phase $\alpha$
sections.summary: For $Ay'' + By' + Cy = \cos\omega t$, $y_p = M\cos\omega t + N\sin\omega t$ with $M = (C - A\omega^2)/D$, $N = B\omega/D$, $D = (C - A\omega^2)^2 + (B\omega)^2$. In polar form $y_p = G\cos(\omega t - \alpha)$ with gain $G = 1/\sqrt D$ and $\tan\alpha = B\omega/(C - A\omega^2)$.
goals: Match cosine and sine terms to find $M$ and $N$.
Convert to the polar form $G\cos(\omega t - \alpha)$.
Use $\omega_n = \sqrt{C/A}$ and the damping ratio $\zeta = B/\sqrt{4AC}$.

notes.heading: Rectangular form
paragraphs: Damping adds a $y'$ term, which turns cosines into sines, so the trial solution needs both: $y_p = M\cos\omega t + N\sin\omega t$. Substituting and matching the $\cos$ and $\sin$ terms gives two linear equations, $(C - A\omega^2)M + B\omega N = 1$ and $-B\omega M + (C - A\omega^2)N = 0$. Their solution:
$M = \dfrac{C - A\omega^2}{D}, \qquad N = \dfrac{B\omega}{D}, \qquad D = (C - A\omega^2)^2 + (B\omega)^2.$

notes.heading: Polar form
paragraphs: One term is better than two: $M\cos\omega t + N\sin\omega t = G\cos(\omega t - \alpha)$ with $G = \sqrt{M^2 + N^2} = 1/\sqrt D$ and $\tan\alpha = N/M = B\omega/(C - A\omega^2)$. The gain $G$ says how much the amplitude is magnified; the phase lag $\alpha$ says how far the response trails the input.

With $B > 0$ the denominator $D$ is never zero, so there is no true resonance. The gain has a peak at $\omega = \sqrt{C/A - B^2/(2A^2)}$, just below $\omega_n$, only when $B^2 < 2AC$. With stronger damping, $B^2 \ge 2AC$, the gain is largest at $\omega = 0$ and decreases as $\omega$ grows.

notes.heading: The lecture's example
paragraphs: $y'' + y' + 2y = \cos t$: $C - A\omega^2 = 2 - 1 = 1$ and $B\omega = 1$, so $D = 2$ and $M = N = \tfrac12$. Then $G = 1/\sqrt2$ and $\alpha = \pi/4$: $y_p = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cos(t - \tfrac{\pi}{4})$.

notes.heading: Better letters
paragraphs: Two combinations carry the physics: the natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{C/A}$ and the damping ratio $\zeta = \dfrac{B}{\sqrt{4AC}}$, which has no units. Engineers write the equation as $y'' + 2\zeta\omega_n y' + \omega_n^2y = f/A$.

quiz.question: A mass $m = 2$ on a spring with $k = 18$ and no damping oscillates at what natural frequency $\omega_n$?

choices.why: No. $3/(2\pi)$ is the frequency in hertz, cycles per second.
Right. $\omega_n = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{9} = 3$.
No. $9$ is $\omega_n^2 = k/m$; take the square root.
No. Divide $k$ by $m$, do not multiply.

quiz.question: For $y'' + \omega_n^2 y = 0$, what is the coefficient of $\sin\omega_n t$?

choices.why: No. Differentiating the sine brings out a factor $\omega_n$.
No. $y(0)$ is the cosine coefficient.
No. You divide by $\omega_n$, not multiply.
Right. The derivative of $c_2\sin\omega_n t$ at $0$ is $c_2\omega_n$, which must equal $y'(0)$.

quiz.question: For $my'' + ky = \cos\omega t$ with $\omega \neq \omega_n$, what is the particular solution?

choices.why: Right. $-m\omega^2Y + kY = 1$ and $k = m\omega_n^2$.
No. The sign is reversed: $k - m\omega^2 = m(\omega_n^2 - \omega^2)$.
No. Without a $y'$ term no sine is needed: $N = 0$.
No. The response follows the driving frequency $\omega$.

quiz.question: Why is $my'' + ky = \delta(t)$ from rest the same as a null problem with $g(0) = 0$, $g'(0) = 1/m$?

choices.why: No. Position starts at $0$; it is the velocity that jumps.

choices.text: It is not; the delta adds a particular solution $1/k$.
choices.why: No. $1/k$ would answer a constant force, a step.

choices.text: The impulse changes the momentum $mg'$ by $1$ instantly, while the position has no time to move.
choices.why: Right. Integrating the equation across $t = 0$ gives a jump of $1$ in $mg'$; afterwards there is no force.
No. The delta function is not a number at $0$; its integral is $1$.
No. $25 - 16 > 0$: overdamped, roots $-1$ and $-4$.
No. $B = 0$: undamped.
Right. $B^2 - 4AC = 16 - 16 = 0$: double root $s = -2$.
No. $4 - 20 < 0$: underdamped.

quiz.question: When $As^2 + Bs + C$ has a double root $s_1$, what is the second null solution?

choices.why: No. A second order equation always has two independent null solutions.
Right. A double root gives $e^{s_1t}$ and $te^{s_1t}$.
No. $2s_1$ is not a root.
No. $-s_1$ is not a root either.

quiz.question: What is the impulse response of $y'' + 3y' + 2y$?

choices.why: No. That starts at $g(0) = 2$, but $g(0)$ must be $0$.
No. That is the step response $r$, the integral of $g$.
No. That is for a double root.

quiz.question: With damping ($B > 0$, $C > 0$), what value does the step response of $y'' + By' + Cy = H(t)$ approach?

choices.why: Right. The constant particular solution $1/C$ remains when the null part decays.
No. That is only when $C = 1$, as on the lecture's board.
No. The step keeps pushing; the impulse response goes to $0$.
No. With $y' = y'' = 0$ the equation reads $Cy = 1$.

quiz.question: What is a particular solution of $y'' - y = e^{t}$?

choices.why: No. Resonance changes the form to $te^{t}$; it does not prevent a solution.
Right. $P(s) = s^2 - 1$ vanishes at $s = 1$, and $P'(1) = 2$, so $y_p = te^t/2$.
No. $e^t$ is a null solution, so it gives zero on the left side.
No. Divide by $P'(1) = 2$.

quiz.question: For $y'' + y' + 2y = \cos t$, what are the gain $G$ and lag $\alpha$?

choices.why: No. Damping makes the response lag: $\tan\alpha = N/M = 1$.
No. That would need $C - A\omega^2 = 0$.
Right. $D = 1^2 + 1^2 = 2$, $M = N = \tfrac12$, and $\tan\alpha = 1$.
No. $\tfrac12$ is $M$ (and $N$); $G = \sqrt{M^2 + N^2}$.
